question: We're putting up an EP for someone joining our trading desk (financial services), and I'm trying to work out what salary to put in the application so the salary part of the scoring isn't a problem. Is there one number we have to hit, and does it count the whole package or just the base?
expected_answer: For the salary criterion (C1) in the EP scoring framework, what is assessed is the candidate's fixed monthly salary — not the total package figure you might quote in an offer letter — and MOM has a separate definition of what counts as fixed monthly salary, so only components that fall within that definition can be counted. The requirement is that this fixed monthly salary meets or exceeds the 65th percentile of local PMET salaries in your sector. That means there is no single across-the-board figure: the benchmark is sector-specific, so your trading-desk hire is measured against the financial services PMET benchmark rather than a general or all-sector one, and a candidate on the same salary could clear the bar in one sector but not in another. Beyond the fixed monthly salary having to meet or exceed that sector's 65th-percentile benchmark, no further conditions on the salary criterion are stated here.

question: I've accepted an offer in Singapore and the pass they're applying for runs two years, but my contract with the firm is longer than that — so at some point it'll need to be extended, sometime in 2026 by my reckoning. Is extending it something I do myself once I'm there, and will I be assessed the same way I was for the first application?
expected_answer: Extending the pass is not something you do yourself — it is the employer who applies to renew an Employment Pass, and they do so if they want you to continue working for them. As for the standard applied: because your pass would be expiring in 2026, i.e. on or after 1 September 2024, the renewal will have to pass the COMPASS requirements. (COMPASS applies to renewals where the EP is expiring from 1 September 2024 onwards; the material here does not set out what the COMPASS requirements consist of, nor any other renewal conditions, so you would need the detailed renewal criteria for that.)

question: One of our senior hires is on an EP with us and we're moving him over to the ONE Pass. His wife is here on a Work Permit with another employer. Two things I'm unsure about: at what point do we cancel his EP, and does she have to stop working in the meantime?
expected_answer:
Timing of the EP cancellation: do not cancel his existing work pass when you submit the ONE Pass application. You should only have the work pass cancelled after the Overseas Networks & Expertise Pass application has been approved and when he is ready to have the ONE Pass issued. Note the consequence of cancelling early — once the work pass is cancelled, he is not permitted to work at all until the ONE Pass is actually issued to him, so there should be no gap between cancellation and issuance.

The spouse: her existing status does not carry over automatically. Once his Overseas Networks & Expertise Pass is approved, you/he will need to reapply for a Dependant's Pass for her, and that DP application takes 4 weeks to process. Because of that processing time she should make the necessary arrangements with her employer for her work during the transition — i.e. plan for the interval rather than assume she can keep working uninterrupted on the old arrangement. (Separate MOM FAQs cover a spouse of a ONE Pass holder applying for a Letter of Consent to work, including multiple LOCs and being both a business owner and an employee, but the details of those are not set out here.)

question: I'm relocating to Singapore on the ONE Pass and my partner would come with me on a long-term visit pass — we've been together years but never legally married. She's already got a firm job offer from a Singapore company, and my mother would also be joining us on a visit pass and might do some part-time work later. Does my partner have to sort out her own work permission, or does the hiring company do it, and would the same route work for my mum?
expected_answer:
Your partner, as a common-law spouse holding a Long-Term Visit Pass, can work on a Letter of Consent (LOC) rather than needing her own work pass — but she does not apply for it herself. The application is made by her prospective employer, who carries out the steps on her behalf: the employer downloads and completes the Letter of Consent (Common-Law Spouse) application form from MOM's website, and then submits that completed form together with the relevant supporting documents online through MOM's submission link (go.gov.sg/mom-submit-loc-cls). So the practical answer for her is: get the firm offer, and have the hiring company lodge the LOC application with the supporting documents.

Your mother is in a different position. The Letter of Consent route is only available to Long-Term Visit Pass holders who are common-law spouses. Any other Long-Term Visit Pass holder — which includes a parent on an LTVP — is not eligible for an LOC and must obtain a work pass in their own right in order to work in Singapore, whether the work is full-time or part-time. The source does not set out processing times, validity periods or further conditions beyond these.
